questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Stating the problem in one sentence
questions.learningObjective: separate a problem statement from a proposed remedy
questions.stem: A team is asked to improve late homework submission. Which sentence states the problem rather than the chosen remedy?

The team will build a web form that uploads work and stamps a time
options.misconception: believes naming the form to build is the same as stating the problem

The tempting answer is the one naming a web form, because a remedy silently assumes the diagnosis is already agreed, and here nothing has been agreed yet.

options.misconception: believes a side effect elsewhere is part of the precondition

options.misconception: believes one pass over a list can rewrite every entry in place

options.text: Report the largest entry, which needs the earlier entries kept in view

options.text: Build a new list holding only the entries above a threshold
options.misconception: believes growing a list requires visiting entries twice

0 is displayed, because the loop always overwrites the discount at the end
options.misconception: believes the final pass wins whatever it tested

options.misconception: believes a threshold list assigns the value it compares against

questions.learningObjective: trace a helper that selects the middle of three values
questions.stem: Trace this helper and state the value it displays. days <- [3, 9, 5]. a <- days[0]. b <- days[1]. c <- days[2]. mid <- a. IF (a < b AND b < c) OR (c < b AND b < a) { mid <- b } ELSE IF (a < c AND c < b) OR (b < c AND c < a) { mid <- c }. DISPLAY mid.

options.text: 5 is displayed, because the second test recognises the third value as the middle
3 is displayed, because the starting value survives both tests failing
options.misconception: believes the initial value also survives the second test

options.text: 9 is displayed, because the largest of the three counts as the typical day
options.misconception: believes the helper finds the largest value not the middle

options.text: 4 is displayed, because the helper averages the three values into the answer
options.misconception: believes comparing values inside a helper implies averaging

questions.stem: A plan has 3 steps of 4 minutes, 2 steps of 6 minutes, and 1 step of 9 minutes. How many minutes do all the steps take?

options.text: 33 minutes, because 12 plus 12 plus 9 comes to thirty-three
27 minutes, because the 9 minute step is counted inside the 6 minute group
options.misconception: believes the nine minute step already sits inside the six minute group

options.text: 36 minutes, because every one of the 6 steps costs the same 6 minutes
options.misconception: believes every step costs the same as the most common one

options.text: 24 minutes, because the step counts are added and the costs ignored
options.misconception: believes adding the step counts gives the total cost

questions.explanation: Three steps at 4 minutes is 12, two at 6 is 12, and one at 9 is 9, and 12 plus 12 plus 9 comes to 33. Each group is priced with its own rate, which is the whole point of grouping them. The tempting answer adds the step counts and ignores the rates, and it lands on a total that looks tidy and understates the plan by nearly a third, which is the kind of gap a schedule only discovers in week two.
questions.hint: Multiply each count by its own cost, then add the three group totals.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a plan should record first
questions.learningObjective: choose the facts a plan needs before coding starts
questions.stem: Two people will review this plan. Which TWO things belong in it before anyone starts coding? Select exactly two.

options.text: The inputs each step receives and the value that step produces
The name of the programming language the team will choose
options.misconception: believes the language choice is information a plan must carry

options.text: The postcondition of each routine that another routine calls
The line numbers of the files each routine will live in
options.misconception: believes file positions belong in a plan reviewers read

questions.explanation: What a step consumes and what it produces is the interface between steps, and a postcondition is the promise a called routine makes, so both let a reviewer trace the plan on paper. The tempting choices are the language and the file positions, which are real decisions but not ones a reviewer can check the logic against, and knowing them adds nothing to the question of whether the steps fit together.
questions.hint: Ask which two facts let a reviewer check the plan without running it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: What a smoke test catches cheaply
questions.learningObjective: choose the faults a first run is most likely to reveal
questions.stem: A feature is about to have its first end-to-end run. Which TWO faults would that run most likely catch? Select exactly two.

options.text: A field name that does not match the data, leaving it unreadable
A colour choice that the team later finds slightly off
options.misconception: believes a tidy diff is the best guard on a behaviour change

options.text: A missing check that lets an empty list reach code expecting data
A routine that needs three passes instead of two on large input
options.misconception: believes a first run measures running time on large input

questions.explanation: A first end-to-end run exercises real data, so a mismatched field name and a missing guard both surface immediately, before anyone is invested in the code. The colour is a judgement call, and the pass count is a performance question that needs a large input this run will not have. The tempting answer is the colour, because it is easy to see, but easy to see is not the same as easy to catch now, and a run is a poor place to review taste.
questions.hint: Ask which faults only appear when real data flows through the whole path.

questions.topic: Habits that make a plan cheap to change
questions.learningObjective: select practices that keep later edits small
questions.stem: A plan will certainly change after it is built. Which TWO habits keep that change cheap? Select exactly two.

options.text: Keeping each task small, so one edit touches only a few steps
Writing every task inside the largest routine in the program
options.misconception: believes one huge routine makes any change local

options.text: Recording in writing what each task is meant to produce
Delaying the first test until every task has been written
options.misconception: believes a later first test makes later changes cheaper

questions.explanation: Small tasks bound the blast radius of an edit, and a written record of what each task produces tells the next reader which parts of the plan the change invalidates. Both are cheap now and pay off at the first revision. The tempting choices are the giant routine and the late first test, and both feel tidy at the time, but they convert one small change into a change to a single large thing nobody fully understands.
questions.hint: Ask which two choices limit how much of the plan one edit reaches.

questions.topic: Order of turning an idea into a slice
questions.learningObjective: sequence the work that turns an idea into a demonstration
questions.stem: Put these actions in the order a team performs them when turning a rough idea into a demonstrable slice.

options.text: Split the chosen feature into one path that runs from input to output
Decide which outcome the feature is meant to change for someone
Build that one path and put it in front of a real user
Write out the design of the screens and reports it left out

questions.explanation: The outcome comes first because it is the thing being tested, then one end-to-end path gives something to build, then a real user finds out what was wrong with the idea, and only then is the rest of the design worth writing. Designing the whole feature first is what the order deliberately avoids. The tempting inversion puts the design work at the front, which feels like progress and produces a document nobody has seen work.
questions.hint: Begin with the outcome, not with the screens, and demo before the rest.

questions.topic: Order of writing down a plan
questions.learningObjective: sequence the steps that turn a goal into a written plan
questions.stem: Put these actions in the order a team performs them while turning a goal into a written plan.

options.text: Build every part and test the finished program once at the end
Write down what each part consumes and what it produces
Break the goal into parts small enough to build in one sitting
Agree what the program will not do, and record those limits

questions.explanation: Exclusions come first because they are what the breakdown is judged against, then the goal divides into parts, then each part gets its interface written down, and only then is anything built. A plan built before the exclusions are agreed grows while it is being written. The tempting order starts with the build, which skips the two steps that make the build checkable and leaves a program nobody can say is finished.
questions.hint: Cut the scope before you cut the work into pieces.

questions.topic: Reading which subtask unblocks the rest
questions.learningObjective: read a plan table to find the subtask others wait on
questions.stem: A plan records five subtasks with the days they need and what waits on each: A takes 3 days and nothing waits on it, B takes 1 and waits on A, C takes 4 and waits on A, D takes 2 and waits on B and C, E takes 1 and waits on D. Which subtask should start first?

options.text: Subtask A, because it is the longest wait and two later parts queue behind it
Subtask D, because it sits at the end of the chain and blocks nobody
options.misconception: believes the end of a chain is the right place to start

options.text: Subtask B, because proving the shortest task first builds confidence
options.misconception: believes the shortest task should always be started first

options.text: Subtask C, because it is the longest task and long tasks start first
options.misconception: believes the longest task must start first whatever waits on it

questions.explanation: Two of the four remaining subtasks wait on A, and A also costs three days, so finishing it releases the most waiting time for the cost of the second-longest task. C is longer but releases only D, so it earns its place second. The tempting answer takes the longest task on sight, which throws away the dependency column the table went to the trouble of recording, and a plan scheduled that way discovers its own bottleneck in the last week.
questions.hint: Find the subtask that the most other subtasks are waiting on.

questions.topic: Reading a value and effort table
questions.learningObjective: read a feature table to pick the cheapest large win
questions.stem: A backlog table lists four features with the number of users affected and the days of work: A has 12 users and 3 days, B has 3 users and 1 day, C has 12 users and 10 days, D has 3 users and 5 days. Which is the clear first choice?

options.text: Feature A, since it reaches as many users as C for a third of the work
Feature B, since finishing the smallest task first is quickest
options.misconception: believes the cheapest task is the best first delivery

options.text: Feature C, since it reaches the most users of anything in the table
options.misconception: believes the widest reach overrides the work needed

options.text: Feature D, since the hardest feature should be cleared out first
options.misconception: believes difficulty is a reason to build something early

questions.explanation: A and C reach the same 12 users, and A costs 3 days against C's 10, so A delivers the same reach for a third of the effort and leaves room to revisit C later. Both columns matter and only the ratio between them decides. The tempting answer is C, which wins one column and loses the other badly, and taking the widest reach first means the team spends ten days before anyone sees anything they can react to.
questions.hint: Compare users reached against days of work, not either column alone.

questions.learningObjective: rank the rows of a table by rate rather than by count
questions.stem: A pilot logged complaints for 1,000 sessions: Home 2, Search 9, Results 4, Settings 1. Which screen should the team look at first?

options.text: Search, because it accounts for the largest share of all complaints
Home, because it is the first screen and every session sees it
options.misconception: believes the first screen a user sees is where a fault must be

options.text: Results, because complaints about results feel more serious
options.misconception: believes a complaint that sounds more serious is the likelier fault

options.text: Settings, because a complaint about it is the rarest of all
options.misconception: believes the rarest complaint is the most informative

questions.explanation: Search produced 9 of the 16 complaints logged, so it carries the largest share and the most evidence of a real problem, and a screen with a repeatable fault beats a louder-sounding one. Counts alone mislead when reach differs. The tempting answer is Home, which looks important because it is first, but two complaints spread over a thousand sessions is a much smaller rate, and prominence in a menu is not evidence of a fault.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.learningObjective: argue that a plan step can be removed and name what to check first
questions.stem: A plan lists six subtasks, one of which writes a summary line to a log file. Explain, in a short paragraph, why cutting that subtask looks safe and what should be checked before it is cut.

answer.exemplar: Cutting the step looks safe because nothing else in the plan reads the log back, and no later step passes a value through it, so removing it leaves every printed value identical. What has to be checked first is whether any person or process outside the program reads the file, and whether the log is named in the group's own runbook. If something outside reads it, the step is not dead, merely invisible from the plan, and removing it changes behaviour that the plan never described. A good answer therefore pairs the claim of safety with the single check that would confirm it, and does not simply assert that nobody reads logs.

questions.explanation: A strong answer names that the step is dead only if nothing outside the program reads the file, points at the runbook or a colleague as the place to check that, and treats the log as behaviour until proven otherwise. An answer that only says nobody reads the log is unsupported, because the plan was written by the team and the reader is the one who may know otherwise. The best answers also note that a step with no observable effect can still be the only record of a failure.
questions.hint: Ask who outside the program might read the file the step writes.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Explaining why equal output is not enough
questions.learningObjective: argue that matching output does not settle which plan to keep
questions.stem: Two different plans for the same feature print identical values for every input tried so far. Explain, in a short paragraph, why that fact alone cannot decide which plan the team keeps.

answer.exemplar: The inputs tried so far only sample the cases the team thought of, so identical output is evidence about that sample and not about the two plans. A plan can match on every sampled input and still differ on an empty list, an unusually large value, or an input that arrives in a different order. Deciding needs a second source of evidence: an input chosen because the two plans disagree, which is found by reading where their steps differ, or a stated requirement that one of them satisfies and the other does not. A good answer says which inputs would separate the two and why agreement on the rest is uninformative.

questions.explanation: A strong answer distinguishes agreement on the cases tried from agreement in general, then names a case that would separate the two plans, such as an empty list or a boundary value. An answer that stops at more testing is too weak, since the point is which testing separates the plans rather than simply running more of it. The strongest answers also connect the choice to a stated requirement, because that is the only thing that makes one plan wrong rather than merely different.
questions.hint: Ask which input the two plans would answer differently on.

questions.learningObjective: pair a requirement with the test that settles it
questions.stem: A club wants late work flagged automatically. Two sentences are offered as requirements. Which one is testable, and what test settles it?

options.text: Any submission after the deadline is flagged; submit one minute late and check
The program should be fair to students; ask three students for a rating
options.misconception: believes a question to users settles a statement about behaviour

options.text: The program will use the house error style; open the source and look
options.misconception: believes a check of the source settles a requirement

options.text: The program will be rewritten next term; run the old version twice
options.misconception: believes comparing two versions of the same build settles intent

questions.explanation: This pair names a condition, a consequence, and a single check that produces one verdict twice over, which is exactly what a requirement and its test look like together. The others each pair an unfalsifiable wish with a check that cannot produce a pass or fail. The tempting pair is the one about fairness, which sounds like the real concern, but asking students how fair they found it measures their impression, not whether a submission was flagged, and the two can easily disagree.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence names a behaviour and an observable result.

questions.topic: Choosing the plan that is cheaper to change
questions.learningObjective: compare two plans by how far a later edit reaches
questions.stem: Two plans for a shop price discount are compared. Which plan is cheaper to change when the rates change, and why?

options.text: The rules live in one routine, so a change reaches a single place only
Each caller repeats the rules, so a change reaches a longer routine
options.misconception: believes repeating a rule in every caller keeps changes together

options.text: The rules are inlined into each caller, so fewer routines need running
options.misconception: believes a shorter call path is the same as a cheaper edit

options.text: The rates are copied into each caller, so duplication makes it clearer
options.misconception: believes copying the same rule twice improves the reader's view

questions.explanation: A change of rate lands in one place in this plan and in three places in the other, so the cost of the change is the number of sites that must agree, and one site cannot disagree with itself. The tempting answer prefers the repeated version because each routine is short and reads clearly, which is a real benefit, but it is bought by making every future rate change a three-site edit that must be found by hand.
questions.hint: Count how many places the new rate would have to be written.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Writing assumptions so they can be checked
questions.learningObjective: judge which practice for recording assumptions holds up
questions.stem: Four teams describe how they treat the assumptions in their plans. Which practice holds up best?

options.text: Each assumption names something a named person could check and be wrong
Assumptions are deleted once the first version of the feature is running
options.misconception: believes a belief stops mattering once code exists

options.text: Assumptions are kept out of the plan until the team agrees on them
options.misconception: believes unrecorded assumptions are safer than recorded ones

options.text: Assumptions are recorded only for the steps that are hardest to build
options.misconception: believes only the difficult steps depend on beliefs

questions.explanation: An assumption is worth writing down only if someone could find out it is wrong, and naming the check and the person makes that possible while the design is still cheap to change. The other three practices all reduce the number of assumptions anyone can confront. The tempting answer is the one about difficult steps, which sounds targeted, but a cheap step resting on a false belief is just as capable of shipping a wrong result, and it is usually harder to trace back.
questions.hint: Ask which practice would let the plan fail loudly instead of quietly.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Critiquing a requirement about the future
questions.learningObjective: find the missing part of a requirement about future changes
questions.stem: A requirement says the program will keep working if the file format later changes. Which criticism of it is strongest?

options.text: It never says where the change would be noticed or what would then happen
A requirement about the future cannot honestly be written at all
options.misconception: belishes that forward-looking requirements are impossible

options.text: File formats belong to the code, so no requirement may mention them
options.misconception: believes requirements should never name anything technical

options.text: It is worded at too great a length for any reader to check once
options.misconception: believes length is the defect rather than a missing condition

questions.explanation: The sentence promises a property without saying what would detect the change or which part of the program would react, so a tester cannot construct a case that would show the promise being met or broken. That missing clause is the substance of the criticism. The tempting answer objects to promising anything about the future, but designing for a change is ordinary work, and refusing to promise it is a decision to be surprised rather than a reason the requirement is unusable.
questions.hint: Ask what the program would have to do when the format does change.
